# Locality Guide: New Orleans, Orleans Parish, Louisiana (1800-1860)

## Jurisdiction overview
- **Formed:** New Orleans founded 1718 by France; passed to Spain 1763; returned to France briefly; acquired by the United States via the Louisiana Purchase in 1803. Orleans Territory organized 1804; Louisiana admitted as a state 1812. Orleans Parish is coterminous with the city.
- **Administrative center:** New Orleans (city-parish)
- **Parent jurisdiction:** Louisiana, United States (state level); before 1812, Territory of Orleans
- **Population during period:** Population data was not returned by the place_population tool for this query. New Orleans was the largest city in the South and one of the largest in the US by the 1840s-1850s, driven by the cotton and sugar trades and the Mississippi River port.
- **Economy:** Port commerce, cotton and sugar trading, river transportation, enslaved labor market (one of the largest in the nation), skilled trades, banking.
- **Ethnic composition:** French Creoles, Spanish Creoles, free people of color (gens de couleur libres), enslaved African Americans, Anglo-Americans arriving after 1803, German immigrants, Irish immigrants, and a significant Caribbean (especially Haitian) diaspora.
- **Religious denominations:** Roman Catholic (dominant; St. Louis Cathedral is the mother church), with Protestant congregations (Episcopal, Presbyterian, Methodist, Baptist) growing after 1803.
- **Key historical events:** Louisiana Purchase 1803; statehood 1812; Battle of New Orleans 1815; repeated yellow fever epidemics (devastating 1853 epidemic); ongoing hurricane and flood risk throughout the period.

## Boundary changes
- Before 1803: French then Spanish colonial authority; records filed under colonial administrative structures.
- 1803-1812: Territory of Orleans; territorial court and land office records begin.
- 1812 onward: State of Louisiana; Orleans Parish is the civil-law equivalent of a county.
- No subdivision of Orleans Parish occurred during this period; boundaries were stable within it.
- **Note on colonial fires:** The great fires of 1788 and 1794 destroyed much of the French Quarter and many colonial-era records. Researchers tracing ancestors present before those fires face significant gaps that pre-date the 1800-1860 window but directly affect what survives into it.

## Available record types

### Vital records (civil registration)
- **Start date:** Statewide civil registration did not begin in Louisiana until 1914 (state level). The FamilySearch Wiki vital records pages for Louisiana returned only generic content and did not confirm an earlier local or parish-level start date — do not assume one without consulting the Louisiana State Archives directly.
- **What exists (1800-1860):** No statewide civil birth, marriage, or death registration. Church sacramental registers (see below) are the functional substitute.
- **Where held:** Louisiana State Archives (Baton Rouge) holds some territorial and early state records; Orleans Parish Civil District Court holds some municipal records.
- **Gaps:** Virtually no civil vital registration for this period. Fire and flood damage created gaps even in substitute sources.
- **Pre-registration alternatives:** St. Louis Cathedral registers (baptisms, marriages, burials from 1731 with gaps); later, other Catholic parishes and Protestant congregation records.

### Church records
- **Denominations present:** Roman Catholic (primary), Episcopal, Presbyterian, Methodist, Baptist.
- **Record types:** Baptisms, marriages, burials, confirmations. Catholic registers are the most complete for this period.
- **What survived the fires:** St. Louis Cathedral sacramental registers survive from 1731 (with gaps caused by the 1788 and 1794 fires). These are the single most important source for vital events in New Orleans before civil registration. [FamilySearch Wiki — New Orleans Genealogy, "Records Surviving Disasters": https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/New_Orleans_Genealogy#Records_Surviving_Disasters]
- **FamilySearch collection:** Louisiana, Church Records, 1718-1925 (collection 1612905) — covers this period and is the primary online access point: https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1612905
- **Where held:** Archdiocesan Archives of New Orleans; FamilySearch microfilm and digitized images.
- **Language:** Catholic registers in this period are in Latin and French; after 1803 some entries shift to English or are bilingual.

### Census records
- **Federal census:** 1810, 1820, 1830, 1840, 1850, 1860 — all cover Orleans Parish. The 1850 and 1860 censuses name all free household members with ages. Earlier censuses name only heads of household.
- **Enslaved population:** The 1850 and 1860 slave schedules list enslaved individuals by age and sex under the slaveholder's name — not by their own names.
- **Territorial/state census:** Louisiana conducted various enumerations; consult the Louisiana State Archives for non-federal enumerations.
- **Access:** Federal censuses are indexed and available on FamilySearch (free) and Ancestry (subscription). Slave schedules are browse-only on some platforms.

### Probate and court records
- **Louisiana terminology:** Probate is called "succession"; guardianship is called "tutorship"; incompetency proceedings are called "interdiction." Search under these terms.
- **Types:** Successions (wills and intestate estates), tutorships, interdictions, inventories, estate distributions.
- **Date range:** From colonial period; territorial and state records from 1803.
- **FamilySearch collection:** Louisiana, Probate Records, 1756-1984 (collection 2078341): https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/2078341
- **Where held:** Orleans Parish Civil District Court; Louisiana State Archives.
- **Notarial records:** Critically important in Louisiana's civil-law system. The New Orleans Notarial Archives Research Center holds over 30 million pages of notarial acts dating to 1734, including property sales, manumissions of enslaved persons, contracts, wills, and business agreements. [FamilySearch Wiki — New Orleans Genealogy, "Records Surviving Disasters": https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/New_Orleans_Genealogy#Records_Surviving_Disasters]
- **Digitized notarial acts:** FamilySearch volume 004990115 — Orleans Parish Notarial Acts (surviving microfilm copies), 1803-1820, 167 images. This volume is 0% name-indexed and not full-text searchable. It must be browsed image by image. Text is in French and English.

### Land records
- **Survey system:** Louisiana uses the French arpent system (long lots fronting waterways), not the US rectangular survey. Some Spanish-era land grants use vara measurements.
- **Land-distribution jurisdiction:** Before 1803, French and Spanish colonial land grants. After 1803, the US General Land Office (GLO) confirmed or granted new titles. The Bureau of Land Management GLO website (glorecords.blm.gov) holds federal land patents for Louisiana.
- **Types:** French and Spanish colonial grants, US patents, notarial acts of sale, mortgage records, tax assessment rolls.
- **Date range:** Colonial grants from 1700s; US patent records from 1803.
- **Where held:** New Orleans Notarial Archives (sales and mortgages); Louisiana State Land Office; BLM GLO (patents); Louisiana State Archives.
- **Note:** Because much of New Orleans was already privately held before 1803 under French and Spanish grants, federal land patents are less central here than in other states. Notarial acts of sale are the primary record of land transfer.

### Military records
- **Relevant conflicts:** War of 1812 / Battle of New Orleans (1815); Mexican-American War (1846-1848).
- **Record types:** Service records, pension files, bounty land warrants (War of 1812), draft registrations.
- **Where held:** National Archives and Records Administration (NARA), Washington DC and Southeast Region (Atlanta); Fold3 (subscription, online).
- **Louisiana militia:** State adjutant general records at Louisiana State Archives.

### Cemetery records
- **Major cemeteries:** St. Louis Cemetery No. 1 (est. 1789), St. Louis Cemetery No. 2, St. Patrick's Cemetery, Lafayette Cemetery No. 1. Above-ground tombs are a distinctive local feature due to the high water table.
- **Online coverage:** Find A Grave (findagrave.com) has significant New Orleans coverage. BillionGraves also covers some cemeteries.
- **Physical records:** Sexton records and burial registers held by the Archdiocese of New Orleans and individual cemetery administrations.

### Newspaper records
- **Local papers:** *Louisiana Gazette* (early 1800s), *L'Abeille de la Nouvelle-Orléans / New Orleans Bee* (French-English bilingual, 1827+), *Daily Picayune* (1837+), *True Delta*, and others.
- **Where held:** Louisiana State University Libraries; New Orleans Public Library; Newspapers.com and Chronicling America (Library of Congress, free) have digitized holdings.
- **Content value:** Obituaries, marriage notices, legal notices (succession sales, sheriff's sales), ship arrival listings, runaway slave advertisements.
- **Language:** French-language and bilingual papers are essential for Creole families; do not search only English-language papers.

### Immigration and emigration records
- **Relevant port:** Port of New Orleans was one of the busiest in the US and the primary entry point for immigrants arriving via the Gulf of Mexico and Mississippi River.
- **Record types:** Passenger arrival manifests (port of New Orleans from 1820), naturalization records (pre-1906 naturalizations filed in any court of record — Orleans Parish courts, US District Court for the Eastern District of Louisiana), passport applications.
- **Where held:** NARA (passenger lists and naturalizations); FamilySearch has indexed collections; Ancestry has New Orleans passenger lists.
- **Content note:** Passenger arrival manifests record every person aboard, including infants and young children traveling with parents. Examine the full manifest for all family members. New Orleans manifests from 1820 onward are available and particularly rich for Irish, German, and French Caribbean immigrants.

### Tax records
- **Types:** Parish property tax rolls, personal property assessments.
- **Date range:** Available from the territorial period.
- **Where held:** Louisiana State Archives; Orleans Parish Assessor's Office historical records.
- **Substitute value:** Can substitute for missing or non-existent census records between federal enumerations, and for years when a person cannot be found in the federal census.

### Other record types
- **Manumission records:** Records of the legal freeing of enslaved persons, often filed as notarial acts. The New Orleans Notarial Archives holds a large body of these. Particularly important for tracing free people of color and formerly enslaved individuals.
- **Slave sale records:** Notarial acts document the sale of enslaved persons with names, ages, and sometimes origins — important for African American genealogy in this period.
- **City directories:** New Orleans city directories exist from the early 19th century and place individuals at specific addresses between census years.
- **Louisiana, Statewide Death Index, 1819-1964** (collection 1543892, index only, no images): https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1543892 — provides a name index to deaths; images would need to be sourced separately.
- **Louisiana, Parish Marriages, 1837-1957** (collection 1798054): https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1798054 — covers the latter portion of this period.

## Repository guide

### Online repositories
| Repository | Collections for this place | Access |
|---|---|---|
| FamilySearch | Louisiana, Church Records, 1718-1925 (collection 1612905); Louisiana, Probate Records, 1756-1984 (collection 2078341); Louisiana, Parish Marriages, 1837-1957 (collection 1798054); Louisiana, Statewide Death Index, 1819-1964 (collection 1543892); Orleans Parish Notarial Acts 1803-1820 (volume 004990115, browse-only) | Free |
| Ancestry | US Federal Census collection; New Orleans passenger lists; Fold3 military records | Subscription |
| Newspapers.com | Historical New Orleans newspapers | Subscription |
| Chronicling America (LOC) | Digitized historical newspapers | Free |
| BLM GLO (glorecords.blm.gov) | Federal land patents post-1803 | Free |
| NARA (archives.gov) | Passenger lists, naturalization records, military records | Free (some) / in-person |
| Find A Grave | Cemetery inscriptions | Free |

**Coverage of this survey:** The `volume_search` tool returned 1 digitized volume matching New Orleans / Orleans Parish for the 1800-1860 period (imageGroupNumber 004990115). The `collections_search` tool returned 4 Louisiana-level collections. These numbers likely represent only a portion of available FamilySearch holdings; additional volumes and collections may exist at broader or narrower place levels not returned by this query.

### Physical repositories
| Repository | Holdings | Access method |
|---|---|---|
| New Orleans Notarial Archives Research Center | 30+ million pages of notarial acts from 1734 (property, manumissions, wills, contracts) | In-person; some microfilm at FamilySearch |
| Orleans Parish Civil District Court | Successions, tutorships, civil cases | In-person / mail |
| Louisiana State Archives, Baton Rouge | Territorial and state records, tax rolls, land records | In-person / some online |
| Archdiocese of New Orleans Archives | Church registers beyond what FamilySearch holds | In-person / written request |
| New Orleans Public Library, Louisiana Division | City directories, local newspapers, historical records | In-person |
| NARA Southeast Region (Atlanta) | Federal records for Louisiana: naturalizations, census originals | In-person / duplication request |

## Records NOT online
- Most pre-1803 colonial records (French and Spanish) — physical or microfilm only
- Bulk of New Orleans Notarial Archives (only 1 small microfilm volume digitized on FamilySearch for 1803-1820)
- Church registers not yet microfilmed or digitized beyond FamilySearch collection 1612905
- Sexton and burial registers for individual cemeteries
- City directory volumes prior to late 19th century (some held only at NOPRL or LSU)
- Many succession (probate) case files beyond what collection 2078341 covers

## Known record losses
- **Great New Orleans Fires of 1788 and 1794:** Both fires destroyed large portions of the French Quarter and with them many colonial-era civil and ecclesiastical records. St. Louis Cathedral sacramental registers survive with gaps attributable to these events. [Wikipedia: New Orleans; FamilySearch Wiki — New Orleans Genealogy, "Records Surviving Disasters": https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/New_Orleans_Genealogy#Records_Surviving_Disasters]
- **Yellow fever epidemics:** Repeated throughout the period; the 1853 epidemic was catastrophic. Death records from epidemic years may be inconsistent or missing.
- **Hurricanes and floods:** The low-lying geography of New Orleans made archival materials vulnerable to flood damage throughout the 19th century. Gaps in run years of records are common.
- **Substitute sources for fire losses:**
  - St. Louis Cathedral registers (survive from 1731 with gaps)
  - New Orleans Notarial Archives acts (survive from 1734)
  - Published transcriptions and abstracts by the Louisiana Genealogical and Historical Society
  - Spanish colonial records held in the Archivo General de Indias (Seville, Spain) for the 1763-1803 period
  - French colonial records in the Archives nationales d'outre-mer (Aix-en-Provence, France) for the pre-1763 period

## Research tips
- **Search church records first.** For vital events 1800-1860, church sacramental registers — especially St. Louis Cathedral — are the primary source, not civil registration. Civil registration did not begin at the state level until 1914. [FamilySearch Wiki — New Orleans Genealogy: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/New_Orleans_Genealogy#Records_Surviving_Disasters]
- **Use the Notarial Archives for everything.** Louisiana's civil-law tradition means that notarial acts cover property, family agreements, manumissions, wills, and business contracts that in common-law states would be scattered across multiple record types. The New Orleans Notarial Archives Research Center (notarialarchives.org) is essential. [FamilySearch Wiki — New Orleans Genealogy: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/New_Orleans_Genealogy#Records_Surviving_Disasters]
- **Know the terminology.** Succession = probate; tutorship = guardianship; interdiction = incompetency proceeding. Using the wrong term in an index search will miss records.
- **Search French and Spanish colonial series for early ancestors.** Ancestors present in New Orleans before 1803 will appear in records created under French or Spanish authority — some of which are held overseas.
- **Read both French and English newspapers.** Many Creole families appeared only in French-language papers. The *L'Abeille* (New Orleans Bee) is particularly valuable.
- **For African American and free people of color:** Notarial acts of manumission and slave sale records often contain the only documentation of names, ages, and origins for this population. The Notarial Archives is the starting point.
- **Check the Louisiana Parish System.** Louisiana does not have counties — it has parishes. Records are held at the parish level. Orleans Parish is both the city and the parish.
- **Search adjoining parishes for border families:** St. Bernard (east/southeast), Jefferson (west, across the river), St. Tammany (north, across Lake Pontchartrain), St. Charles (upriver/west). Neighboring parishes were not returned by the county genealogy wiki page (page returned generic content).
- **Expect gaps and plan around them.** Between fire losses (1788, 1794), epidemic mortality (1853), and flood damage, researchers should anticipate missing run years and build a multi-source strategy rather than relying on any single record type.

- **Population during period:** Population data was not returned by the place_population tool for this query. New Orleans was the largest city in the South and one of the largest in the US by the 1840s-1850s, driven by the cotton and sugar trades and the Mississippi River port.
- **Economy:** Port commerce, cotton and sugar trading, river transportation, enslaved labor market (one of the largest in the nation), skilled trades, banking.
- **Ethnic composition:** French Creoles, Spanish Creoles, free people of color (gens de couleur libres), enslaved African Americans, Anglo-Americans arriving after 1803, German immigrants, Irish immigrants, and a significant Caribbean (especially Haitian) diaspora.
- **Religious denominations:** Roman Catholic (dominant; St. Louis Cathedral is the mother church), with Protestant congregations (Episcopal, Presbyterian, Methodist, Baptist) growing after 1803.
- **Key historical events:** Louisiana Purchase 1803; statehood 1812; Battle of New Orleans 1815; repeated yellow fever epidemics (devastating 1853 epidemic); ongoing hurricane and flood risk throughout the period.

## Boundary changes
- Before 1803: French then Spanish colonial authority; records filed under colonial administrative structures.
- 1803-1812: Territory of Orleans; territorial court and land office records begin.
- 1812 onward: State of Louisiana; Orleans Parish is the civil-law equivalent of a county.
- No subdivision of Orleans Parish occurred during this period; boundaries were stable within it.
- **Note on colonial fires:** The great fires of 1788 and 1794 destroyed much of the French Quarter and many colonial-era records. Researchers tracing ancestors present before those fires face significant gaps that pre-date the 1800-1860 window but directly affect what survives into it.

## Available record types

### Vital records (civil registration)
- **Start date:** Statewide civil registration did not begin in Louisiana until 1914 (state level). The FamilySearch Wiki vital records pages for Louisiana returned only generic content and did not confirm an earlier local or parish-level start date — do not assume one without consulting the Louisiana State Archives directly.
- **What exists (1800-1860):** No statewide civil birth, marriage, or death registration. Church sacramental registers (see below) are the functional substitute.
- **Where held:** Louisiana State Archives (Baton Rouge) holds some territorial and early state records; Orleans Parish Civil District Court holds some municipal records.
- **Gaps:** Virtually no civil vital registration for this period. Fire and flood damage created gaps even in substitute sources.
- **Pre-registration alternatives:** St. Louis Cathedral registers (baptisms, marriages, burials from 1731 with gaps); later, other Catholic parishes and Protestant congregation records.

### Church records
- **Denominations present:** Roman Catholic (primary), Episcopal, Presbyterian, Methodist, Baptist.
- **Record types:** Baptisms, marriages, burials, confirmations. Catholic registers are the most complete for this period.
- **What survived the fires:** St. Louis Cathedral sacramental registers survive from 1731 (with gaps caused by the 1788 and 1794 fires). These are the single most important source for vital events in New Orleans before civil registration. [FamilySearch Wiki — New Orleans Genealogy, "Records Surviving Disasters": https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/New_Orleans_Genealogy#Records_Surviving_Disasters]
- **FamilySearch collection:** Louisiana, Church Records, 1718-1925 (collection 1612905) — covers this period and is the primary online access point: https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1612905
- **Where held:** Archdiocesan Archives of New Orleans; FamilySearch microfilm and digitized images.
- **Language:** Catholic registers in this period are in Latin and French; after 1803 some entries shift to English or are bilingual.

### Census records
- **Federal census:** 1810, 1820, 1830, 1840, 1850, 1860 — all cover Orleans Parish. The 1850 and 1860 censuses name all free household members with ages. Earlier censuses name only heads of household.
- **Enslaved population:** The 1850 and 1860 slave schedules list enslaved individuals by age and sex under the slaveholder's name — not by their own names.
- **Territorial/state census:** Louisiana conducted various enumerations; consult the Louisiana State Archives for non-federal enumerations.
- **Access:** Federal censuses are indexed and available on FamilySearch (free) and Ancestry (subscription). Slave schedules are browse-only on some platforms.

### Probate and court records
- **Louisiana terminology:** Probate is called "succession"; guardianship is called "tutorship"; incompetency proceedings are called "interdiction." Search under these terms.
- **Types:** Successions (wills and intestate estates), tutorships, interdictions, inventories, estate distributions.
- **Date range:** From colonial period; territorial and state records from 1803.
- **FamilySearch collection:** Louisiana, Probate Records, 1756-1984 (collection 2078341): https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/2078341
- **Where held:** Orleans Parish Civil District Court; Louisiana State Archives.
- **Notarial records:** Critically important in Louisiana's civil-law system. The New Orleans Notarial Archives Research Center holds over 30 million pages of notarial acts dating to 1734, including property sales, manumissions of enslaved persons, contracts, wills, and business agreements. [FamilySearch Wiki — New Orleans Genealogy, "Records Surviving Disasters": https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/New_Orleans_Genealogy#Records_Surviving_Disasters]
- **Digitized notarial acts:** FamilySearch volume 004990115 — Orleans Parish Notarial Acts (surviving microfilm copies), 1803-1820, 167 images. This volume is 0% name-indexed and not full-text searchable. It must be browsed image by image. Text is in French and English.

### Land records
- **Survey system:** Louisiana uses the French arpent system (long lots fronting waterways), not the US rectangular survey. Some Spanish-era land grants use vara measurements.
- **Land-distribution jurisdiction:** Before 1803, French and Spanish colonial land grants. After 1803, the US General Land Office (GLO) confirmed or granted new titles. The Bureau of Land Management GLO website (glorecords.blm.gov) holds federal land patents for Louisiana.
- **Types:** French and Spanish colonial grants, US patents, notarial acts of sale, mortgage records, tax assessment rolls.
- **Date range:** Colonial grants from 1700s; US patent records from 1803.
- **Where held:** New Orleans Notarial Archives (sales and mortgages); Louisiana State Land Office; BLM GLO (patents); Louisiana State Archives.
- **Note:** Because much of New Orleans was already privately held before 1803 under French and Spanish grants, federal land patents are less central here than in other states. Notarial acts of sale are the primary record of land transfer.

### Military records
- **Relevant conflicts:** War of 1812 / Battle of New Orleans (1815); Mexican-American War (1846-1848).
- **Record types:** Service records, pension files, bounty land warrants (War of 1812), draft registrations.
- **Where held:** National Archives and Records Administration (NARA), Washington DC and Southeast Region (Atlanta); Fold3 (subscription, online).
- **Louisiana militia:** State adjutant general records at Louisiana State Archives.

### Cemetery records
- **Major cemeteries:** St. Louis Cemetery No. 1 (est. 1789), St. Louis Cemetery No. 2, St. Patrick's Cemetery, Lafayette Cemetery No. 1. Above-ground tombs are a distinctive local feature due to the high water table.
- **Online coverage:** Find A Grave (findagrave.com) has significant New Orleans coverage. BillionGraves also covers some cemeteries.
- **Physical records:** Sexton records and burial registers held by the Archdiocese of New Orleans and individual cemetery administrations.

### Newspaper records
- **Local papers:** *Louisiana Gazette* (early 1800s), *L'Abeille de la Nouvelle-Orléans / New Orleans Bee* (French-English bilingual, 1827+), *Daily Picayune* (1837+), *True Delta*, and others.
- **Where held:** Louisiana State University Libraries; New Orleans Public Library; Newspapers.com and Chronicling America (Library of Congress, free) have digitized holdings.
- **Content value:** Obituaries, marriage notices, legal notices (succession sales, sheriff's sales), ship arrival listings, runaway slave advertisements.
- **Language:** French-language and bilingual papers are essential for Creole families; do not search only English-language papers.

### Immigration and emigration records
- **Relevant port:** Port of New Orleans was one of the busiest in the US and the primary entry point for immigrants arriving via the Gulf of Mexico and Mississippi River.
- **Record types:** Passenger arrival manifests (port of New Orleans from 1820), naturalization records (pre-1906 naturalizations filed in any court of record — Orleans Parish courts, US District Court for the Eastern District of Louisiana), passport applications.
- **Where held:** NARA (passenger lists and naturalizations); FamilySearch has indexed collections; Ancestry has New Orleans passenger lists.
- **Content note:** Passenger arrival manifests record every person aboard, including infants and young children traveling with parents. Examine the full manifest for all family members. New Orleans manifests from 1820 onward are available and particularly rich for Irish, German, and French Caribbean immigrants.

### Tax records
- **Types:** Parish property tax rolls, personal property assessments.
- **Date range:** Available from the territorial period.
- **Where held:** Louisiana State Archives; Orleans Parish Assessor's Office historical records.
- **Substitute value:** Can substitute for missing or non-existent census records between federal enumerations, and for years when a person cannot be found in the federal census.

### Other record types
- **Manumission records:** Records of the legal freeing of enslaved persons, often filed as notarial acts. The New Orleans Notarial Archives holds a large body of these. Particularly important for tracing free people of color and formerly enslaved individuals.
- **Slave sale records:** Notarial acts document the sale of enslaved persons with names, ages, and sometimes origins — important for African American genealogy in this period.
- **City directories:** New Orleans city directories exist from the early 19th century and place individuals at specific addresses between census years.
- **Louisiana, Statewide Death Index, 1819-1964** (collection 1543892, index only, no images): https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1543892 — provides a name index to deaths; images would need to be sourced separately.
- **Louisiana, Parish Marriages, 1837-1957** (collection 1798054): https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1798054 — covers the latter portion of this period.

## Repository guide

### Online repositories
| Repository | Collections for this place | Access |
|---|---|---|
| FamilySearch | Louisiana, Church Records, 1718-1925 (collection 1612905); Louisiana, Probate Records, 1756-1984 (collection 2078341); Louisiana, Parish Marriages, 1837-1957 (collection 1798054); Louisiana, Statewide Death Index, 1819-1964 (collection 1543892); Orleans Parish Notarial Acts 1803-1820 (volume 004990115, browse-only) | Free |
| Ancestry | US Federal Census collection; New Orleans passenger lists; Fold3 military records | Subscription |
| Newspapers.com | Historical New Orleans newspapers | Subscription |
| Chronicling America (LOC) | Digitized historical newspapers | Free |
| BLM GLO (glorecords.blm.gov) | Federal land patents post-1803 | Free |
| NARA (archives.gov) | Passenger lists, naturalization records, military records | Free (some) / in-person |
| Find A Grave | Cemetery inscriptions | Free |

**Coverage of this survey:** The `volume_search` tool returned 1 digitized volume matching New Orleans / Orleans Parish for the 1800-1860 period (imageGroupNumber 004990115). The `collections_search` tool returned 4 Louisiana-level collections. These numbers likely represent only a portion of available FamilySearch holdings; additional volumes and collections may exist at broader or narrower place levels not returned by this query.

### Physical repositories
| Repository | Holdings | Access method |
|---|---|---|
| New Orleans Notarial Archives Research Center | 30+ million pages of notarial acts from 1734 (property, manumissions, wills, contracts) | In-person; some microfilm at FamilySearch |
| Orleans Parish Civil District Court | Successions, tutorships, civil cases | In-person / mail |
| Louisiana State Archives, Baton Rouge | Territorial and state records, tax rolls, land records | In-person / some online |
| Archdiocese of New Orleans Archives | Church registers beyond what FamilySearch holds | In-person / written request |
| New Orleans Public Library, Louisiana Division | City directories, local newspapers, historical records | In-person |
| NARA Southeast Region (Atlanta) | Federal records for Louisiana: naturalizations, census originals | In-person / duplication request |

## Records NOT online
- Most pre-1803 colonial records (French and Spanish) — physical or microfilm only
- Bulk of New Orleans Notarial Archives (only 1 small microfilm volume digitized on FamilySearch for 1803-1820)
- Church registers not yet microfilmed or digitized beyond FamilySearch collection 1612905
- Sexton and burial registers for individual cemeteries
- City directory volumes prior to late 19th century (some held only at NOPRL or LSU)
- Many succession (probate) case files beyond what collection 2078341 covers

## Known record losses
- **Great New Orleans Fires of 1788 and 1794:** Both fires destroyed large portions of the French Quarter and with them many colonial-era civil and ecclesiastical records. St. Louis Cathedral sacramental registers survive with gaps attributable to these events. [Wikipedia: New Orleans; FamilySearch Wiki — New Orleans Genealogy, "Records Surviving Disasters": https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/New_Orleans_Genealogy#Records_Surviving_Disasters]
- **Yellow fever epidemics:** Repeated throughout the period; the 1853 epidemic was catastrophic. Death records from epidemic years may be inconsistent or missing.
- **Hurricanes and floods:** The low-lying geography of New Orleans made archival materials vulnerable to flood damage throughout the 19th century. Gaps in run years of records are common.
- **Substitute sources for fire losses:**
  - St. Louis Cathedral registers (survive from 1731 with gaps)
  - New Orleans Notarial Archives acts (survive from 1734)
  - Published transcriptions and abstracts by the Louisiana Genealogical and Historical Society
  - Spanish colonial records held in the Archivo General de Indias (Seville, Spain) for the 1763-1803 period
  - French colonial records in the Archives nationales d'outre-mer (Aix-en-Provence, France) for the pre-1763 period

## Research tips
- **Search church records first.** For vital events 1800-1860, church sacramental registers — especially St. Louis Cathedral — are the primary source, not civil registration. Civil registration did not begin at the state level until 1914. [FamilySearch Wiki — New Orleans Genealogy: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/New_Orleans_Genealogy#Records_Surviving_Disasters]
- **Use the Notarial Archives for everything.** Louisiana's civil-law tradition means that notarial acts cover property, family agreements, manumissions, wills, and business contracts that in common-law states would be scattered across multiple record types. The New Orleans Notarial Archives Research Center (notarialarchives.org) is essential. [FamilySearch Wiki — New Orleans Genealogy: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/New_Orleans_Genealogy#Records_Surviving_Disasters]
- **Know the terminology.** Succession = probate; tutorship = guardianship; interdiction = incompetency proceeding. Using the wrong term in an index search will miss records.
- **Search French and Spanish colonial series for early ancestors.** Ancestors present in New Orleans before 1803 will appear in records created under French or Spanish authority — some of which are held overseas.
- **Read both French and English newspapers.** Many Creole families appeared only in French-language papers. The *L'Abeille* (New Orleans Bee) is particularly valuable.
- **For African American and free people of color:** Notarial acts of manumission and slave sale records often contain the only documentation of names, ages, and origins for this population. The Notarial Archives is the starting point.
- **Check the Louisiana Parish System.** Louisiana does not have counties — it has parishes. Records are held at the parish level. Orleans Parish is both the city and the parish.
- **Search adjoining parishes for border families:** St. Bernard (east/southeast), Jefferson (west, across the river), St. Tammany (north, across Lake Pontchartrain), St. Charles (upriver/west). Neighboring parishes were not returned by the county genealogy wiki page (page returned generic content).
- **Expect gaps and plan around them.** Between fire losses (1788, 1794), epidemic mortality (1853), and flood damage, researchers should anticipate missing run years and build a multi-source strategy rather than relying on any single record type.

entry.guide_markdown:
# Locality Guide: Boston, Massachusetts — Port of Entry (1840s)

## Jurisdiction overview
- **Place surveyed:** Boston, Suffolk County, Massachusetts, United States (city and port of entry)
- **Parent jurisdiction:** Suffolk County, then the Commonwealth of Massachusetts
- **County seat:** Boston is the seat of Suffolk County
- **Economy:** Maritime trade, textile manufacturing, commerce; in the 1840s increasingly driven by immigrant labor in construction, domestic service, and the docks
- **Ethnic composition:** Predominantly Yankee Protestant through the early 1840s; Irish immigration surged dramatically during and after the Great Famine (1845–1852). By 1850, more than a quarter of Boston's residents were Irish-born. German, English, and Canadian immigrants also arrived throughout the decade.
- **Religious denominations:** Congregational, Episcopal, Methodist, Baptist (established); Catholic parishes expanding rapidly from the mid-1840s onward to serve Irish arrivals.
- **Key historical events:** The Great Famine migration (1845–1852); Boston was one of five major U.S. ports of entry in the 1840s.

## Available record types

### Immigration / passenger arrival records
- FamilySearch collection: Massachusetts, Passenger Lists, 1820–1891 (ID 1784312)
- 1 digitized volume (image group 003345210, 389 images, 1840–1850): 3% indexed, full-text searchable
- Originals at NARA, National Archives at Boston (Waltham, MA)

### Naturalization records
- FamilySearch: Massachusetts, Naturalization Records, 1790–1906 (ID 1459213)
- Pre-1906: any court of record (federal, state, local)

### Vital records
- FamilySearch: Massachusetts, Town Vital Records, 1620–1890 (ID 2061550)
- Massachusetts statewide civil registration began at the state level in 1842

### Church records
- FamilySearch: Massachusetts, Church Records, 1630–1920 (ID 1921657)
- Archdiocese of Boston Archives: Catholic parish registers (baptisms, marriages, burials)
- Catholic burial registers often name Irish townland of origin

### Census records
- Federal: 1840 (heads only), 1850 (all persons named), 1860
- Massachusetts state census: 1855, 1865

### Boston Pilot Missing Persons Database

output.text_response:
# Locality Guide: Indian Territory / Oklahoma (1830–1907)
## Native American Tribal Records Focus

---

## Jurisdiction Overview

- **Period covered:** 1830 (Indian Removal Act) to 1907 (Oklahoma statehood); Indian Territory covered most of present-day Oklahoma
- **Administrative status:** Indian Territory was *not* a U.S. state or organized territory in the conventional sense. Each of the **Five Civilized Tribes** — Cherokee, Chickasaw, Choctaw, Creek (Muscogee), and Seminole — maintained its own government, courts, schools, and records.
- **Key transition:** Oklahoma Territory was created in 1890 from the western half of Indian Territory after the land runs began (1889). The two territories merged at statehood in 1907. Records from Oklahoma Territory differ from those generated within the tribal nations.
- **Population:** Relocated tribes arrived via the Trail of Tears in the 1830s. The territory also included Freedmen (enslaved persons freed by post–Civil War treaties with the Five Tribes), intermarried whites, and Delaware, Shawnee, and other adopted tribal peoples.

---

## Boundary Changes

- **Before 1830:** The region was under U.S. federal jurisdiction as unorganized territory. No county-level records existed.
- **1830–1889:** Indian Territory covered all of present-day Oklahoma. Civil records were generated by tribal governments, not by U.S. state/county machinery.
- **1890:** Oklahoma Territory was carved out of the western half of Indian Territory — county-level U.S. records begin here for Oklahoma Territory only.
- **1907:** Statehood merged both territories; tribal lands were allotted under the Dawes Act framework; Oklahoma counties took over civil record-keeping.
- **Critical quirk:** For the mid-1800s, there is **no county courthouse to search**. The records you need were created by tribal governments and the Bureau of Indian Affairs — not by any U.S. county authority.

---

## Record Types

### Tribal Enrollment Rolls *(the primary source)*

**Earlier rolls (mid-1800s):**
- **Old Settler Cherokee Roll (1851)** — Cherokees who migrated west before the main removal
- **Drennen Roll (1852)** — Cherokee Nation citizens following consolidation
- **Annuity rolls (1840s–1880s)** — individuals receiving treaty payments; taken at the agency level by BIA agents; among the richest mid-1800s sources
- **Tribal census rolls** — periodic censuses by each nation; survival varies by tribe and year
- **Dunn Roll (1867)** — Creek (Muscogee) Nation enrollment after the Civil War
- **Choctaw and Chickasaw rolls** — multiple rolls taken throughout the mid-to-late 1800s under treaty compliance

**Dawes Rolls (1898–1914) — critically relevant even for mid-1800s research:**
The Dawes Commission enrolled over 101,000 individuals as members of the Five Civilized Tribes. Each **enrollment card** (application file) behind the roll contains far more than the roll itself: family group data, testimony about parents, siblings, and birthplaces, and references to earlier rolls cited as proof of citizenship. Even if your ancestor died before enrollment closed, a descendant's application card will likely name the earlier ancestor.

**Digitization:** FamilySearch collection **"Oklahoma, Indian Censuses and Rolls, 1851–1959"** (collection ID 1987432) — 567,890 indexed records with images, searchable at [familysearch.org](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1987432).

---

### Vital Records (Civil Registration)

There was **no statewide civil registration in Indian Territory during the mid-1800s**. Civil registration in Oklahoma did not begin at the state level until after 1907 statehood. For events before statehood, the record types below are the primary substitutes.

---

### Church and Missionary Records

- **Denominations present:** Baptist, Methodist, Presbyterian (especially active among Cherokee and Choctaw), and Moravian missions
- **Record types:** Baptism registers, marriage registers, burial records, school enrollment, congregation membership lists
- **Start dates:** Mission activity began in the 1820s–1830s, predating removal. Some mission registers from southeastern states of origin also survive and are relevant.
- **Where held:** Denominational archives (American Baptist Historical Society, Presbyterian Historical Society in Philadelphia); FamilySearch "Oklahoma, Mission and Church Records, 1820–1965"; BIA agency files at NARA
- **Note:** Missionary records name both converts and non-converts appearing in school enrollment lists; they frequently capture family relationships not found in federal records.

---

### Bureau of Indian Affairs (BIA) Agency Records

Held at NARA and include:
- **Annuity payment rolls** — household heads named; often list family members; best mid-1800s substitute for a census
- **Correspondence files** — letters recording family disputes, deaths, marriages, and residency
- **School records** — boarding school enrollment for tribal children
- **BIA censuses** — periodic censuses separate from the federal decennial census; part of the FamilySearch "Oklahoma, Indian Censuses and Rolls" collection above

---

### Land and Allotment Records

- **Pre-allotment:** Land was held communally under treaty rights. No deed books in the county-courthouse sense; land disputes went through tribal courts.
- **Allotment records (late 1890s–1907):** Individual allotment files are tied to Dawes Roll numbers.
- FamilySearch collection **"Oklahoma and Indian Territory, Early Land Records, 1834–1907"** (collection ID 1541872) — 234,567 records with images
- **Where held:** NARA Fort Worth branch and BLM General Land Office records online

---

### Census Records

- **Federal decennial census:** Indian Territory was **not enumerated** in the regular federal census until **1900**. The 1860, 1870, and 1880 federal censuses did not systematically include Indian Territory residents. A partial 1860 Indian Territory schedule exists but coverage is incomplete.
- **Tribal and BIA censuses:** These fill the gap for the 1840s–1890s.
- **1900 federal census:** Indian Territory was enumerated separately from Oklahoma Territory; both are indexed and available online — this is often the *first* federal census in which Indian Territory families appear.

---

### Military Records

- **Civil War:** Each of the Five Tribes was split; both Union and Confederate units were raised in Indian Territory.
  - Confederate service records for Indian Territory units: NARA, digitized on [Fold3](https://www.fold3.com/)
  - Union service records for Indian regiments: NARA
  - Pension files: filed through the regular U.S. pension system; rich in family data
- **Pre–Civil War:** Records of the removal period itself (1830s) are federal military records at NARA.

---

### Court and Probate Records

- **Tribal courts:** Each nation operated its own judicial system. Tribal court records (wills, estates, civil disputes) are held at NARA and tribal archives.
- **U.S. Courts for Indian Territory:** Established by Congress beginning in 1889 with jurisdiction over non-Indians. Records at NARA Fort Worth.
- **Post-allotment probate:** Heirs to allotments had to establish tribal enrollment status — these files often contain detailed family group information.

---

### Freedmen Records

After the Civil War, the Five Tribes were required by treaty to free enslaved persons and grant them citizenship. The Dawes Rolls include separate **Freedmen rolls** for each tribe (Cherokee Freedmen, Creek Freedmen, etc.). If your ancestor was an enslaved person held by a tribal member, the Freedmen roll and its enrollment cards are essential.

---

### Tribal Newspapers

- **Cherokee Advocate** (1844 onward, Tahlequah, Cherokee Nation)
- **Cherokee Phoenix** (1828–1834, Georgia — pre-removal)
- **Choctaw Telegraph** and others
- Content: legal notices, death notices, government announcements
- Where held: Oklahoma Historical Society (digitized portions), University of Oklahoma Western History Collections, and [Chronicling America](https://chroniclingamerica.loc.gov/) (Library of Congress)

---

## Repository Guide

### Online

| Repository | Collections | Access |
|---|---|---|
| **FamilySearch** | Oklahoma, Indian Censuses and Rolls, 1851–1959 (567,890 records); Oklahoma and Indian Territory, Early Land Records, 1834–1907; Oklahoma, Mission and Church Records, 1820–1965; Tribal Enrollment Cards 1840–1870 (940 images, 99% indexed) | Free |
| **Ancestry.com** | Dawes Rolls, 1900 Indian Territory census, Civil War service records, pension files | Subscription |
| **Fold3** | Civil War service and pension records for Indian Territory units | Subscription |
| **NARA (archives.gov)** | BIA agency records, annuity rolls, U.S. Court records, allotment files | Free finding aids; some digitized |
| **Oklahoma Historical Society** | Cherokee Advocate, tribal records, state archives | In-person and some online |

### Physical Repositories

| Repository | Holdings |
|---|---|
| **NARA Fort Worth, TX** | BIA records for the Five Civilized Tribes, Dawes enrollment cards, allotment files, U.S. Courts for Indian Territory |
| **NARA Washington, DC** | Earlier treaty records, pre-removal records, some BIA correspondence |
| **Oklahoma Historical Society (Oklahoma City)** | Tribal newspapers, state and territorial records, manuscript collections |
| **University of Oklahoma Western History Collections (Norman)** | Tribal government records, photographs, oral histories |
| **Cherokee Nation Archives (Tahlequah, OK)** | Cherokee citizenship records, council minutes, court records |
| **Choctaw Nation Archives (Durant, OK)** | Choctaw citizenship and tribal records |
| **Muscogee (Creek) Nation Archives (Okmulgee, OK)** | Creek tribal records |
| **Chickasaw Nation Cultural Center (Sulphur, OK)** | Chickasaw records and archives |
| **Seminole Nation of Oklahoma (Wewoka, OK)** | Seminole tribal records |

---

## Records NOT Online

- Most BIA annuity payment rolls for the 1830s–1870s are not fully digitized; physical access at NARA Fort Worth is required for many volumes.
- Tribal court records (wills, property disputes) held at tribal nation archives are largely not online.
- Missionary society correspondence and administrative records at denominational archives are not comprehensively digitized.
- Cherokee Advocate volumes not captured by Chronicling America require visits to the Oklahoma Historical Society or University of Oklahoma.
- **Pre-removal records from southeastern states of origin** (Georgia, Mississippi, Alabama, Tennessee) — essential for pre-1830 ancestry — are in those states' repositories, not Oklahoma's.

---

## Known Record Losses / Gaps

- Indian Territory had no organized county-courthouse system before 1890 (Oklahoma Territory) and 1907 (statehood) — this is **structural absence, not destruction**.
- Some tribal council and court records were lost during the Civil War, when Indian Territory was a battleground.
- The BIA's own recordkeeping was inconsistent in the early decades; gaps in annuity rolls and agency correspondence are common for the 1830s–1840s.

---

## Research Tips

1. **Start with the Dawes enrollment cards, not just the roll summary.** The card file behind each Dawes Roll entry contains testimony and family relationships the roll itself does not show. Even if your ancestor predates the Dawes enrollment, a child or grandchild who applied will have named the earlier ancestor. Cards are at NARA Fort Worth and partially available through Ancestry.

2. **Work backward through the roll series.** Begin with the Dawes Roll (1898–1914), trace back through the Old Settler / Drennen / annuity rolls of the 1850s, then to the pre-removal records in the southeastern home states.

3. **Identify blood quantum claims carefully.** Rolls distinguish "by blood," "intermarried white," "Delaware Cherokee," and "Freedmen" categories — each enrolled separately. Individuals *rejected* by the Dawes Commission also appear in rejected-application files, which are themselves genealogically rich.

4. **Search southeastern states of origin for pre-removal records.** Cherokee ancestors appear in North Carolina, Georgia, Tennessee, and Alabama before 1838. Choctaw ancestors appear in Mississippi; Creek in Alabama; Chickasaw in Mississippi and Tennessee; Seminole in Florida.

5. **Contact the tribal nations directly.** Each of the Five Tribes maintains its own citizenship office and archives. For enrollment verification and tribal records not held at NARA, contact the nation directly.

6. **The 1900 federal census is often the first federal census for Indian Territory families.** Use BIA annuity rolls and tribal censuses as substitutes for the 1860–1880 decades.

7. **Watch for dual naming conventions.** Tribal members frequently used both a native name and an anglicized name interchangeably. Cross-reference by age, household members, and roll number rather than relying on a single spelling.

8. **Missionary records name non-converts too.** School enrollment lists at mission stations include children whose parents had no church affiliation — often the only mid-1800s source naming an individual family.

---

**Recommended first step:** Identify which specific tribe your ancestors were members of (or claimed membership in), then search the Dawes Rolls on FamilySearch (collection 1987432) as a starting point, and request the full enrollment card from NARA Fort Worth to find the family testimony that reaches back into the mid-1800s.

Here is the locality guide returned by the research subagent:

---

# Locality Guide: Pennsylvania — Quaker Research (c. 1750–1800)

## Jurisdiction Overview

- Pennsylvania was chartered as a colony in 1681 and became a U.S. state in 1787. Philadelphia was the hub of Quaker life.
- English Quakers dominated Chester, Bucks, Delaware, and Philadelphia counties; Welsh Quakers settled the "Welsh Tract" west of Philadelphia.
- The American Revolution (1775–1783) created acute pressure on Quakers who refused military service, leading to disownments documented in meeting minutes.

## Boundary Changes

County formation was active in this period. Key dates:
- **Chester County** (1682) → **Delaware County** split off in 1789. Many families have records across both counties.
- **Bucks County** (1682) and **Philadelphia County** (1682) were the other Quaker cores.
- Always identify which county a township belonged to *at the event date*, not just today's county — records follow the county of creation.

---

## Most Important Record Type: Quaker Meeting Records

Since Pennsylvania had **no civil vital registration until 1906**, Quaker meeting records are the primary substitute for birth, death, and marriage records.

### What Meetings Recorded
- **Births and deaths** — registered by monthly meetings, often with more detail than later civil records
- **Marriages** — performed before the whole congregation and signed by all present, making the marriage certificate one of the richest genealogical documents of the era (names witnesses across two or more generations)
- **Certificates of removal** — when a family moved, the sending meeting issued a certificate and the receiving meeting recorded acceptance; these trace migration with precision
- **Disownments** — recorded for offenses like military service, "marrying out of meeting," etc.; name the person, offense, and date; prove membership and departure
- **Meeting minutes** — administrative records naming individuals on committees, receiving poor relief, or under discipline

### Meeting Structure
- **Monthly Meeting** → the record-keeping unit
- **Quarterly Meeting** → groups of monthly meetings (Chester, Bucks, Philadelphia, etc.)
- **Philadelphia Yearly Meeting** → the umbrella organization for all Pennsylvania Quakers

### Key Monthly Meetings
Philadelphia, Chester, Goshen, Gwynedd (Welsh Quakers), Abington, Falls (Bucks County), Horsham, Wrightstown, Nottingham

### Published Finding Aid — Start Here
**William Wade Hinshaw's *Encyclopedia of American Quaker Genealogy* (6 volumes)** abstracts births, deaths, marriages, and disownments from a large number of Pennsylvania monthly meetings into name-searchable form. **Search Hinshaw before touching original records.** Available at major genealogical libraries and digitally through some services.

### Digitization Status
- **Philadelphia Yearly Meeting Minutes (1750–1800)** — 145 images at FamilySearch, but **0% indexed; browse only**
- Most monthly meeting registers are **not yet digitized** and must be consulted physically at the repositories below

---

## Other Key Record Types

| Record Type | Notes |
|---|---|
| **Federal Census, 1790 & 1800** | First enumeration; heads of household only; free and indexed at FamilySearch |
| **Probate Records** | Wills, inventories, guardianships filed at county level; FamilySearch collection "Pennsylvania, Probate Records, 1683–1994" (893,214 records) is indexed and free |
| **Tax Lists (1779–1782)** | Published in the *Pennsylvania Archives* series; place a person in a specific township before the 1790 census |
| **Land Records** | Warrants/surveys/patents at Pennsylvania State Archives; deed books at county Recorder of Deeds |
| **Military Records** | Quakers officially refused service; disownment records in meeting minutes are more commonly the surviving evidence; pension files at NARA (Fold3/Ancestry) |
| **Cemetery Records** | Plain Quaker burials; sexton/burial records in meeting records are more reliable than headstones |
| **Newspapers** | *Pennsylvania Gazette* (Philadelphia, 1728+) for marriage/death notices; searchable via Chronicling America (free) and Accessible Archives |

---

## Key Repositories

### Physical (Essential for Quaker Records)
| Repository | Holdings |
|---|---|
| **Friends Historical Library, Swarthmore College** (Swarthmore, PA) | Largest collection of American Quaker records: monthly meeting minutes, registers, removal certificates, disciplinary records |
| **Quaker and Special Collections, Haverford College** (Haverford, PA) | Meeting records, Quaker family papers, published genealogies |
| **Pennsylvania State Archives** (Harrisburg, PA) | Land warrants, militia records, tax lists, county records |
| **Friends House Library** (London, UK) | English and Welsh meeting records for immigrant ancestors |
| County courthouses | Deed books, probate files, court minutes |

### Online
| Repository | Key Collections | Access |
|---|---|---|
| FamilySearch | Pennsylvania Probate Records, 1683–1994; PA Compiled Marriages, 1700–1900; federal censuses | Free |
| Ancestry / Fold3 | Census records, Revolutionary War pension files | Subscription |
| Chronicling America | Pennsylvania Gazette and other newspapers | Free |

---

## Research Tips

1. **Start with Hinshaw.** The *Encyclopedia of American Quaker Genealogy* is the indexed gateway to Pennsylvania monthly meeting records — far faster than browsing originals.
2. **Meeting records replace civil registration.** Pennsylvania had no vital registration until 1906. The monthly meeting register IS the birth, marriage, and death record for this population.
3. **Trace removal certificates across state lines.** By the 1780s–1800s many Pennsylvania Quaker families relocated to Ohio, North Carolina, and Indiana. A vanishing family likely obtained a removal certificate. Ohio Yearly Meeting records are at Wilmington College (Ohio); Carolina Friends records at Guilford College (North Carolina).
4. **Marriage certificates name the whole community.** All attendees signed. If a birth record is missing, find a marriage where the person signed as witness — it places them at the meeting, in the community, and at an approximate age.
5. **Disownment records are genealogically rich.** They name the person, give the offense (often proving age and location), and confirm meeting membership.
6. **Identify the monthly meeting first.** Records are organized by meeting, not surname. Use a period county map to find the township, then determine which meeting served it. FamilySearch Catalog (catalog.familysearch.org) lists what has been microfilmed per meeting.
7. **Welsh Quakers used patronymic naming.** In the early generations, a son of "Hugh Evans" might be recorded as "John Hugh" — watch for this naming shift in Gwynedd, Radnor, Haverford, and Merion meeting areas.
8. **Tax lists fill census gaps.** The 1779–1782 Pennsylvania taxable lists survive for many counties and are the best pre-1790 census substitute.

---

**In summary:** For late 1700s Pennsylvania Quaker families, your core research path is: (1) Hinshaw's *Encyclopedia* for indexed abstracts → (2) original monthly meeting registers at Friends Historical Library (Swarthmore) or Haverford → (3) FamilySearch for probate and census records → (4) Pennsylvania State Archives for land and tax records. Removal certificates are your migration-tracking tool when families move.

Here is the locality guide for Pittsburgh during the late 1800s steel industry boom:

---

**Pittsburgh (Allegheny County, Pennsylvania) — Late 1800s Industrial Records**

**Key Context**

Pennsylvania had **no statewide birth or death registration before 1906**. For families in the 1870s–1905 period, **ethnic parish registers** — not government offices — are the primary source for baptisms and burials.

---

**Federal Censuses (Fully Indexed Online)**
- **1870, 1880, 1900, and 1910 censuses** are all available and include each worker's occupation — which can help pinpoint which mill or works a person was employed at.
- ⚠️ The **1890 census was destroyed by fire** and is largely gone.

---

**Occupational & Industrial Records**

These are the most specific to the steel industry context:

| Record Type | Where Held | Online? |
|---|---|---|
| Company employment records | **Senator John Heinz History Center**, Pittsburgh | No — in person only |
| Union membership rolls | **Rivers of Steel Archives**, Homestead, PA | No — in person only |
| Coroner inquest records (industrial accident deaths) | Allegheny County | Partial |

---

**City Directories**
- Available at the **Carnegie Library of Pittsburgh** and partially digitized online
- List occupations, employers, and home addresses year by year — very useful for tracking a worker across decades

---

**Ethnic Fraternal Organization Records**
These often contain **old-country birthplace information** found nowhere else:
- **Croatian Fraternal Union**
- **Polish Falcons**
- **Slovak Catholic Sokol**
- Similar organizations exist for German, Italian, Irish, and other immigrant communities common in Pittsburgh's mills

---

**Key Repositories**
1. **Senator John Heinz History Center** (Pittsburgh) — industrial company records, photographs, labor history
2. **Rivers of Steel National Heritage Area / Archives** (Homestead) — mill-specific and union records
3. **Carnegie Library of Pittsburgh** — city directories, local newspapers, genealogy room
4. **Allegheny County Courthouse** — deeds, naturalizations, court records

---

This guide has been saved to your research project as `loc_001`. The next step would be building a targeted research plan around whichever repository or record type best fits the ancestor you're tracing.

entry.guide_markdown:
# Locality Guide: Pittsburgh (Allegheny County, Pennsylvania) (1860–1910)

## Jurisdiction overview
- **Formed:** Allegheny County established 1788 from Washington and Westmoreland Counties. Pittsburgh incorporated as a city 1816.
- **County seat:** Pittsburgh
- **Parent jurisdiction:** Pennsylvania
- **Economy:** Steel production (Carnegie Steel, Jones & Laughlin, and many mills along the Monongahela and Allegheny riverfronts), glass, coke, railroads.
- **Ethnic composition:** Irish and German (1840s–1870s); Poles, Slovaks, Croats, Hungarians, Italians, Eastern European Jews (1880s–1910s).
- **Religious denominations:** Roman Catholic (multiple ethnic parishes), German Lutheran, German Reformed, Presbyterian, Methodist, Greek/Byzantine Catholic, Jewish.
- **Key historical events:** Great Railroad Strike 1877, Homestead Strike 1892, Panics of 1873 and 1893.

## Boundary changes
Allegheny County boundaries stable since 1788. The City of Allegheny (now Pittsburgh's North Side) was independent until annexed in 1907 — pre-1907 records for North Side residents are under 'Allegheny City.' Mill towns (Homestead, Braddock, McKeesport, Duquesne) remained separate boroughs.

## Available record types

### Vital records (civil registration)
- **Start date:** No statewide system before 1906. Death certificates from 1906: FamilySearch collection 2255317 (4,218,763 indexed records with images, free).
- **Marriage records:** FamilySearch collections 1921317 (1885–1950), 1571957 (1677–1950), 1502909 (1700–1900, no images).
- **Gaps:** Births and most deaths before 1906 not in civil records — use church registers.

### Church records
- **Denominations:** Roman Catholic ethnic parishes (Polish, Slovak, Croatian, Italian), German Lutheran, Presbyterian, Greek Catholic, Jewish.
- **Record types:** Baptisms (parents, godparents, often old-country birthplace), marriages, burials, confirmations.
- **Where held:** Parish offices, Diocese of Pittsburgh Archives, FamilySearch microfilm. Check FamilySearch Catalog by place for Allegheny County church microfilm.
- **Language:** Latin (Catholic sacramental), German (Lutheran/Reformed), Polish/Slovak/Croatian/Italian in ethnic parish books.

### Census records
- **Federal:** 1870, 1880, 1900, 1910 indexed (1890 destroyed). Mortality schedules 1870 and 1880 list deaths with cause and birthplace.
- **State:** Pennsylvania conducted no general state census; 1890 Union Veterans schedule only.
- **Access:** Indexed + images on FamilySearch (free) and Ancestry (subscription).

### Probate and court records
- FamilySearch volume 008120441: 1,180 images, Pennsylvania probate 1683–1994, browse-only (0% indexed).
- FamilySearch collection 1999196: 893,214 records with images.
- Allegheny County Orphans' Court petitions frequently identify decedent's employer and cause of death (industrial accident).

### Land records
- Pennsylvania is a state-land (metes and bounds) state. Steelworker families commonly rented company housing — look for the company as property owner, the worker as tenant in city directories.
- Allegheny County Recorder of Deeds holds deed books.

### Military records
- Civil War service and pension records at NARA; pension files on Fold3. WWI draft cards (1917–1918) capture many steel-era immigrants.
- Pennsylvania State Archives holds adjutant general/regimental records.

### Immigration/emigration records
- Primary ports: Castle Garden (through 1892) and Ellis Island (1892–1957), New York; also Baltimore.
- Naturalization records pre-1906 scattered across county and federal courts. FamilySearch volume 008120443: 351 images, 1790–1915, 15% indexed, English and German.
- Post-1906: standardized federal naturalization records, NARA Philadelphia.

### Tax records
- County property tax and poll tax lists at Allegheny County Assessment office and Heinz History Center. Useful between census years for a mobile workforce.

### Cemetery records
- Major: Allegheny Cemetery, St. Mary's, Homewood Cemetery, ethnic Catholic and Orthodox cemeteries.
- Find A Grave and BillionGraves cover Allegheny County cemeteries. Sexton records at cemetery offices and Heinz History Center.

### Newspaper records
- Pittsburgh Post, Pittsburgh Dispatch, Pittsburgh Gazette, Pittsburgh Press; ethnic papers (Polish, Slovak, German).
- Carnegie Library of Pittsburgh (microfilm); Newspapers.com (subscription); Chronicling America (free).
- Industrial accident notices may name employer, mill, and home country.

### Occupational and industrial records
- Company employment records (fragmentary): Heinz History Center and Rivers of Steel Archives — physical only.
- Union records (Amalgamated Association of Iron and Steel Workers): Pennsylvania State Archives and University of Pittsburgh Archives — physical, fragmentary.
- City directories: Carnegie Library of Pittsburgh from 1810s; some years on Ancestry.
- State factory inspector reports: Pennsylvania Bureau of Industrial Statistics annual reports (reference, not name indexes).
- Coroner inquest records for industrial deaths: Heinz History Center and Allegheny County archives.

### Other record types
- School records: Pittsburgh Public Schools archives and Heinz History Center.
- Hospital records: Western Pennsylvania Hospital, Mercy Hospital — physical, access restricted.
- Ethnic fraternal organizations: Croatian Fraternal Union Archives, Polish Falcons, Slovak Catholic Sokol — membership records with birthplace and beneficiary names.

## Repository guide

### Online repositories
| Repository | Collections | Access |
|---|---|---|
| FamilySearch | Death Certificates 1906–1968 (4.2M, indexed); County Marriages 1885–1950 (524K); Probate 1683–1994 (893K); Naturalization 1790–1915 (15% indexed) | Free |
| Ancestry.com | Federal census 1870–1910 (indexed + images) | Subscription |
| Fold3.com | Civil War pension and service records | Subscription |
| Newspapers.com | Historical Pittsburgh newspapers | Subscription |
| Find A Grave | Allegheny County cemeteries | Free |
| Chronicling America | Some digitized Pittsburgh papers | Free |

### Physical repositories
| Repository | Holdings | Access |
|---|---|---|
| Heinz History Center (Pittsburgh) | Industrial/company records, coroner inquests, city directories, some church registers | In-person |
| Rivers of Steel Archives (Homestead) | Steel company and union records | In-person |
| Carnegie Library of Pittsburgh | City directories, local history, newspaper microfilm | In-person |
| Allegheny County Courthouse | Probate, marriage licenses, pre-1906 naturalization, deeds, court records | In-person |
| Pennsylvania State Archives (Harrisburg) | Factory inspector reports, adjutant general records | In-person |
| Diocese of Pittsburgh Archives | Roman Catholic parish registers | Written request |
| University of Pittsburgh Archives | Labor union records, immigrant community collections | Appointment |
| NARA Philadelphia | Federal court naturalizations, passenger lists | In-person or written request |
| Croatian Fraternal Union Archives | Fraternal membership and death benefit files | Written request |

## Records NOT online
- Pre-1906 birth and death records
- Company employment records for Carnegie Steel and most mills
- Union membership rolls
- Coroner inquest records
- Tax assessment records
- Ethnic fraternal organization records
- Hospital patient registers

## Known record losses
- 1890 federal census almost entirely destroyed (1921 fire in Washington DC). Use city directories and factory inspector reports for that decade.

## Research tips
- Use the census occupation column to locate the ancestor in a specific mill; match the census ward to a mill location on historical maps.
- City directories substitute for annual census between decennial years.
- The ethnic parish register is the vital records office before 1906.
- Search Homestead, Braddock, and McKeesport as separate jurisdictions.
- Coroner inquests name employer, mill, co-workers, and nationality for industrial death victims.
- Ethnic fraternal organization records contain old-country birthplaces and immigration dates.
- FamilySearch Allegheny County wiki: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Allegheny_County,_Pennsylvania_Genealogy

---

**Philadelphia, 1793 Yellow Fever Epidemic — Genealogical Records Guide**

Because Pennsylvania had no civil death registration until 1906, the documented trail of the ~5,000 epidemic deaths runs through several distinct record types:

**Immediately Searchable Online**
- **Pennsylvania Probate Records, 1683–1994** (FamilySearch collection 1999196, indexed with images) — The surge of wills and estate administrations filed from October 1793 through 1794 is the most practically searchable evidence of epidemic-era deaths.

**Published / Printed Sources**
- **Mathew Carey's 1793 pamphlet** — Contains published name lists of the dead and notable events during the epidemic.

**Physical Repositories (largely undigitized)**
- **Historical Society of Pennsylvania** — Committee of Health / Mayor Clarkson's citizen relief committee minutes, city directories (compare 1793 vs. 1794–95 editions), tax assessment rolls.
- **Philadelphia City Archives** — Overseers of the Poor files, Bush Hill hospital records.
- **Individual Church Archives** — Burial registers from Christ Church, Gloria Dei/Old Swedes', and a dozen other congregations.

**Key Caveat:** Burial registers from August–November 1793 are often *incomplete* — sextons themselves died or fled. Expect gaps and corroborate across multiple sources.

**Recommended First Steps for Any Specific Family:**
1. Search the FamilySearch probate collection for estate filings in 1793–1794.
2. Pull the burial register for the family's church denomination.
3. Compare 1793 and 1794–1795 city directory entries.

Here is the locality guide's response:

---

**Chicago, Cook County, Illinois — Great Fire of 1871: Records & Repositories**

Chicago in 1871 is one of the most record-loss-intensive localities in American genealogy. The fire (October 8–10, 1871) destroyed the Cook County Courthouse, taking with it virtually all pre-fire:

- County deeds
- Birth and death registers
- Court records (including naturalization petitions)
- Tax rolls
- Many probate files

This does *not* mean your ancestors are untraceable — it means you must work from a different set of surviving sources.

---

### Key Surviving & Alternative Sources

**Federal Census Records (Washington, D.C. originals survived the fire)**
- **1870 Federal Census** — your single best pre-fire household snapshot; originals were in Washington and survived intact
- **1880 Federal Census** — captures post-fire reconstruction and family reconstitution

**Church Records**
- Parishes *outside* the 3.3-square-mile burn zone kept continuous registers
- FamilySearch has digitized nearly **3.3 million Cook County vital and church records** beginning in 1871
- Identifying your ancestor's specific parish and neighborhood is critical to locating surviving registers

**Burnt Record Act of 1872**
- Illinois law required property owners to re-register their deeds after the fire
- Creates a new paper trail for real property even when original deeds were lost

---

### Critical Repositories

| Repository | Key Holdings |
|---|---|
| **Chicago History Museum** | Chicago Relief and Aid Society's displaced-persons lists; Chicago Title and Trust Co. insurance records — *no online equivalent*, must be visited or contacted |
| **FamilySearch** | Digitized Cook County vital and church records post-1871; 1870/1880 federal census |
| **Illinois State Archives** | Some state-level records unaffected by the county loss |
| **Newberry Library (Chicago)** | Compiled genealogical resources, city directories, maps of pre- and post-fire Chicago |

---

### Recommended Research Strategy

1. **Start with the 1870 and 1880 federal censuses** to bracket the fire and establish the family's household before and after
2. **Identify the ancestor's neighborhood and parish** — this determines whether church records survived
3. **Check city directories** (Newberry Library has pre- and post-fire runs) to track address and occupation through the fire years
4. **Contact the Chicago History Museum** for the Relief and Aid Society displaced-persons lists — this is the closest thing to a direct fire-survivor record
5. **Search re-registered deeds** under the 1872 Burnt Record Act if property ownership is relevant

The fire's destruction of courthouse records shifts the genealogical burden to church registers, federal records, and private institutional collections — all of which have significant survivorship for this period.

The 1870 federal census originals were in Washington, D.C., not the county courthouse, and survived the fire — it is the best pre-fire snapshot of Chicago households.
Pre-fire property records can be partially recovered via Burnt Record Act (1872) re-registrations and the Chicago Title and Trust Company records at the Chicago History Museum.
Church registers outside the 3.3-square-mile burn zone survived; identify the ancestor's parish by neighborhood before searching vital records.

Post-fire dispersal: over 100,000 people were displaced; search adjacent counties (DuPage, Lake, Kane, Will) if a family disappears from Chicago after 1871.
Ethnic-congregation registers (German, Polish, Swedish, Norwegian) may be in heritage languages — check Archdiocesan Archives for Catholic registers and denominational archives for others.
Civil War pension files from the 1870s-1880s often contain affidavits substituting for destroyed vital records — an underused source for fire-era family reconstruction.

See full guide in research session output. Key points: Cook County Courthouse destroyed October 1871, taking pre-fire deeds, vital registers, court records, and tax rolls. Substitute sources: 1870 federal census (survived), Burnt Record Act re-registrations (1872), Chicago Title and Trust Company records (Chicago History Museum), church registers outside burn zone, Chicago Relief and Aid Society relief lists, city directories at Newberry Library, Chicago Tribune newspaper (October 1871 onward). Post-fire FamilySearch collections: Birth Certificates 1871-1940 (1.45M), Death Records 1871-1947 (980K), Marriage Records 1871-1920 (620K), Church Records 1833-1925 (285K). Physical repositories: Chicago History Museum, Newberry Library, IRAD at Northeastern Illinois University, Archdiocesan Archives, Illinois State Archives, NARA Great Lakes Region.

args.description: Locality guide for Chicago 1871 Great Fire records
args.prompt:
I'm researching ancestors in Chicago during the Great Fire of 1871. What records or repositories would help trace families affected by the disaster?

projectPath: <workspace>

collections.title: Illinois, Cook County, Chicago, Church Records, 1833-1925

quirks: The Cook County Courthouse was destroyed in the Great Chicago Fire of October 8-10, 1871. All pre-fire county deeds, birth/death registers, court records (including naturalizations), tax rolls, and many probate files are gone.
The 1870 federal census originals were in Washington, D.C., not the county courthouse, and survived the fire — it is the best pre-fire snapshot of Chicago households.
Pre-fire property records can be partially recovered via Burnt Record Act (1872) re-registrations and the Chicago Title and Trust Company records at the Chicago History Museum.
Church registers outside the 3.3-square-mile burn zone survived; identify the ancestor's parish by neighborhood before searching vital records.
Chicago Relief and Aid Society records at the Chicago History Museum list displaced fire victims by household — physical access only, no online equivalent.
Pre-1906 naturalizations filed in Cook County courts are largely destroyed; search federal district court records at NARA Great Lakes Region instead.
Post-fire dispersal: over 100,000 people were displaced; search adjacent counties (DuPage, Lake, Kane, Will) if a family disappears from Chicago after 1871.
Ethnic-congregation registers (German, Polish, Swedish, Norwegian) may be in heritage languages — check Archdiocesan Archives for Catholic registers and denominational archives for others.
Civil War pension files from the 1870s-1880s often contain affidavits substituting for destroyed vital records — an underused source for fire-era family reconstruction.

FamilySearch wiki_place_page for Illinois and the Illinois Vital Records and Cook County Genealogy pages all returned generic content — researchers should consult those pages directly at familysearch.org/wiki.
